Abstract 19

The global shift toward net-zero emissions necessitates resource recovery from wet 20

waste. In this study, we demonstrate the first feasibility of combining pilot-scale 21

microbial electrolytic cells (MECs) with hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) for 22

simultaneous post-hydrothermal liquefaction wastewater (PHW) treatment and 23

efficient hydrogen (H₂) production to meet biocrude upgrading requirements. Long- 24

term single reactor operation revealed that fixed anode potential enabled rapid startup, 25

and low catholyte pH and high salinity were effective in suppression of cathodic 26

methanogenesis and acetogenesis – resulting in high current density of 16.6 A m-2 and 27

9.3 A m-2 when feeding synthetic wastewater and PHW respectively. Additionally, the 28

anode biofilm exhibited spatial variations in response to local environmental conditions. 29

Onsite parallel or serial operations of multiple MECs showed good performance using 30

actual PHW with a record-high H2 production rate of 0.5 L LR day-1 for MEC over 10 31

liters scale, and the optimal chemical oxygen demand (COD)-to-H2 yield reached 0.127 32

kg-H2 per kg-COD, supporting a self-sufficient, closed-loop upgrade to jet fuel. 33

1. Introduction 37

As we strive to keep the fossil carbon underground, sustainable biomass emerges as a 38

crucial carbon source to enable carbon circulation and the transition to clean energy, 39

fuels, and chemicals (Jack et al., 2019; Lu and Ren, 2016). The current management 40

practices for wet waste, such as food waste, animal manure, and wastewater sludge, 41

consume significant energy but fail to recover high value products from the embedded 42

energy and carbon (Milbrandt et al., 2018). In this context, hydrothermal liquefaction 43

(HTL) emerged as a promising technology for wet waste treatment and valorization. 44

HTL transforms wet waste into biocrude oil under high pressure and moderate 45

temperature (Alper Basar et al., 2021), and after hydrotreating, the biocrude can be 46

upgraded to sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). SAF is among the most desired products 47

from organic waste, as it has high value and significant market potential, addressing 48

one of the most challenging tasks of aviation sector decarbonization. However, HTL 49

currently faces several major technical challenges. The U.S. Department of Energy 50

identified the management of post-HTL wastewater (PHW) as a key barrier. This 51

wastewater is highly concentrated and contains recalcitrant nitrogen species, which 52

traditional wastewater treatment facilities struggle to treat (Jiang et al., 2023b; Wang et 53

al., 2024; Watson et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020). In addition, a substantial amount of 54

H2 is required to reduce heteroatoms (such as sulfur, nitrogen, and oxygen) in the 55

biocrude oil before it can be refined into SAF (Snowden-Swan et al., 2022). Currently, 56


<!-- Page 4 -->


most H2 supply comes from natural gas, which significantly undermines the 57

sustainability of the overall process (Global Hydrogen Review 2022, 2022). 58

59

Different treatment and valorization techniques have been explored for managing PHW, 60

including biological, hydrothermal, and integrated pathways (Watson et al., 2020). For 61

example, PHW can be used for biomass cultivation to grow algae or crops, with the 62

captured carbon from biomass further utilized as food and biofuel (Zhou et al., 2013). 63

However, this method requires extensive land area, and commonly requires heavy 64

dilution to avoid growth inhibitions (Watson et al., 2020). Alternatively, hydrothermal 65

gasification can be applied to PHW to produce energy-rich gas. Although this process 66

is fast and efficient, it demands a stringent reactor design and high energy input (Watson 67

et al., 2017). Plus, these processes don’t resolve the issue of H2 demand. In this context, 68

integrating microbial electrolysis cells (MECs) with HTL stands out as an especially 69

attractive solution. By leveraging microbial metabolism and electrochemical H2 70

production, MECs can simultaneously treat the recalcitrant wastewater while producing 71

clean H2 for onsite biocrude upgrading, thereby creating a closed-loop process (Fig. 1A) 72

(Jiang et al., 2022; Wang and Ren, 2013). Our previous works demonstrated that lab- 73

scale MECs can produce up to 1.62 L L-1 d-1 H2 using PHW as feedstock, achieving a 74

COD removal rate up to 98% for the recalcitrant stream (Jiang et al., 2023b; Shen et al., 75

2018). However, the real-world potential has not been verified as scaling-up often 76

comes up with unique challenges such as limited current density, and compromised 77


<!-- Page 5 -->


long-term stability (Jiang et al., 2023a). More importantly, the previous scale-up efforts 78

of MEC often produce H2 as a standalone product without a contextual need. Although 79

H2 consumption is expected to increase in the coming decades, finding an onsite use 80

case that balances the supply and demand still holds great advantage as transportation 81

of H2 remains an expensive and emission-intensive process (Global Hydrogen Review 82

2022, 2022; Winter et al., 2022). Therefore, demonstrating a proof-of-concept closed- 83

loop integration with a pilot HTL system would set a precedent for more fit-for-purpose 84

bioelectrochemical H₂ production. 85

86

In this study, we present the first pilot integration of MECs with HTL system. We 87

designed a symmetric rectangular reactor module featuring two anode chambers and 88

one cathode chamber. Each reactor module has a total capacity over 80 liters and a 89

working volume of 55 liters. To assess the suitability of PHW as an MEC substrate and 90

the challenges of scaling up the process, we conducted long-term and onsite operations 91

using actual PHW from HTL reactors processing food waste. Satisfying organic 92

removal and H2 production were obtained, and the close-loop biocrude upgrading 93

without external H2 supply was achieved with optimal COD-to-H2 yield. 94

2. Materials and methods 95

2.1. Pilot MEC assembly 96

In total, four reactor modules were manufactured, one for in-lab long-term 97

operation, and three for onsite operation. Each reactor module (110 cm×13 cm×60 cm) 98

came in rectangular shape with reactor frames manufactured from 99


<!-- Page 6 -->


acrylic.(“Performance of a pilot-scale continuous flow microbial electrolysis cell fed 100

winery wastewater | Applied Microbiology and Biotechnology,” n.d.) Each module was 101

divided into three chambers with two anode chambers (100 cm×4 cm×50 cm each) on 102

the side and one cathode chamber (100 cm×3 cm×50 cm) in the middle. Two back 103

plates (each 1 cm wide) enclosed the chambers by sandwiching the two anode chamber 104

frames and one cathode chamber frame in between. Nineteen carbon brush anodes (60 105

cm long with 10 cm bare end and a carbon brush diameter of 4 cm) were evenly inserted 106

into each anode chamber and were connected by wire connector blocks (Jandeccn) 107

through 14-gauge wires. Before insertion, the carbon anode brushes were heat-treated 108

at 450 ℃ for 30 min.(Feng et al., 2010) Stainless steel wire cloth (316 SS, 60×60 mesh 109

size, 0.009" opening size, McMaster-Carr) were used as cathode. The wire cloth was 110

cut into 78 cm×26 cm size (2,000 cm2 cross section area) and fixed with titanium wire 111

(0.031" Diameter, 1/4 lb. Coil, McMaster-Carr) for connection with potentiostat and 112

power supply. The working volume of each anode and cathode chamber is 20 L and 15 113

L, respectively. The anode chamber and cathode chamber were separated by cation 114

exchange membrane (CXM-200, Membrane International Inc.). Before application, the 115

membrane is first preconditioned in 5% NaCl solution for 12 hours for hydration and 116

expansion. Due to the large cross section area (5,000 cm2) of the module, three 117

supporting structures were evenly distributed in each anode chamber to prevent 118

membrane deformation while minimizing water blockage (Fig. S1). 119

2.2. Pilot HTL and PHW feedstock 121

The PHW was produced from a pilot-scale continuous plug-flow HTL reactor 122

capable of treating 1.5 tons of biowaste and producing 200 L of biocrude per day 123

(Summers et al., 2023; Watson et al., 2021). Two different types of PHW were 124

produced and tested in the study, one from grocery food waste collected from a local 125

grocery store in Champaign, IL (PHW-GFW) and one from salad dressing waste 126

collected from local food processing plant (PHW-SDW). The HTL reaction was carried 127

out under 280 ℃, 12.4 MPa and a retention time of 30 min. The biocrude oil and PHW 128

were separated via gravity and oil skimmers. The produced raw PHW was then further 129

filtered through a filter bag (PEXL-5-P01E-WW-30L, EATON) to remove suspended 130

solids such as oil chunks. The detailed description of the HTL system, and 131

characteristics of the PHW feedstock can be found elsewhere (Summers et al., 2023). 132

2.3. MEC operation 136


<!-- Page 8 -->


For inoculation, anodic effluent containing electroactive bacteria (EABs) from in- 137

lab MECs were mixed with MEC anolyte (1:1 v/v) containing sodium acetate to serve 138

as the inoculum.(Bian et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2023b) The MEC anolyte contains 100 139

mM phosphate buffer solution (PBS, 9.16 g L−1 Na2HPO4 and 4.90 g L−1 NaH2PO4), 140

4.92 g L-1 sodium acetate, mineral solution (12.5 mL L-1) and vitamin solutions (5 mL 141

L-1) (Jiang et al., 2022). Two different inoculation strategies were explored in this study: 142

fixed-voltage and fixed-potential. In fixed-voltage inoculation, 1.2 V was applied 143

across each module by DC power supply (Keithley 2260B-720W) (Lu et al., 2015). In 144

fixed-potential inoculation, the anodes were poised at a constant potential at -0.35 V vs. 145

Ag/AgCl reference electrode using potentiostat (Biologic, France) (Zhu et al., 2022). 146

In both strategies, inoculum was only added at the beginning of the inoculation. 147

148

After successful inoculation, each module was connected to one power supply. The 149

current was recorded by measuring the voltage drop across a 0.1 Ω resistor electrically 150

connected in-series with the module. In lab-scale studies, the voltage across the reactor 151

is often considered equal to the voltage set at the power supply as the voltage loss across 152

the wire and the resistor is negligible. However, this voltage loss due to resistance can 153

be significant at pilot scale as the current is much higher. As a reference, a 1-amp 154

current would lead to 100 mV voltage loss across the 0.1 Ω resistor, a significant loss 155

considering MEC uses relatively small voltages (oftentimes 300 – 1,000 mV). 156

Therefore, the actual voltage across the MEC module is also recorded by potentiostat 157


<!-- Page 9 -->


to account for the loss in the circuit. The cathode gas was collected using a gas bag 158

(Calibrated Instrument) attached to the cathodic chamber. The gas components were 159

analyzed with a gas chromatography with TCD detector (SRI310, SRI Instrument) with 160

UHP N2 as carrier gas (Jack et al., 2022). 161

162

For the long-term operation, one MEC module (R-single) was operated for three months. 163

R-single was operated in a continuous, 100% recirculation manner with an anolyte flow 164

rate of 50 L day-1 and a catholyte flow rate of 20 L day-1. A continuous system would 165

improve mass transfer, but would also bring additional challenges such as increased H2 166

loss and membrane deformation. However, we alleviated membrane deformation 167

through supporting structure (Section 2.1) and did not observe significant H2 loss 168

throughout the experiments. The catholyte was 100 mM PBS, and the anolyte was 169

started with synthetic wastewater during startup then switched to PHW-GFW diluted 170

with 100 mM PBS to maintain influent COD at around 4,000 mg L-1. The anolyte and 171

catholyte were operated with their own liquid loop with automatic pH adjusting with a 172

dosing station, and each loop contains a recirculation bottle as reservoir. The anolyte 173

and catholyte pH were initially all set at 7.0, but the catholyte pH was further dosed 174

down to 4.0 to inhibit acetogens during the operation (see Section 3.1.3 for details). 175

The pH adjustment was done by digital pH controllers (Bluelab, USA) connected to 176

sulfuric acid (50% v/v, for cathode pH control) or sodium hydroxide solution (50% w/v, 177

for anode pH control). The COD was continuously monitored and when the COD value 178


<!-- Page 10 -->


fell under 500 mg L-1, the recirculation bottle was refilled with new substrates. All 179

aqueous solutions were prepared with DI water. 180

181

After gaining insights and experience from R-single operation, onsite pilot operation 182

was carried out. Three identical MEC modules (R1, R2 and R3) were fabricated and 183

operated inside the same building that houses the pilot HTL reactor. Similar operation 184

strategy was implemented, with the EAB cultures inoculated from the R-single reactor 185

and initially enriched with synthetic wastewater. After reactors were stabilized 186

(reaching a platform in current density), they were fed with diluted PHW-SDW that has 187

a COD around 5,000 mg L-1. The cathode liquid loop was operated continuously with 188

100% recirculation and kept at pH = 4 using a pH dosing station. The anode liquid loop 189

was operated continuously without recirculation. Due to the continuous nature, the 190

anolyte did not need pH adjustment during onsite integration. After all three modules 191

stabilized in operation, both in-series and in-parallel operational modes of the anode 192

loop were investigated. During in-parallel operation, each module was applied a voltage 193

of 0.7 V. During in-series operation, R1, R2 and R3 were supplied with 0.9 V, 0.7 V 194

and 0.5 V voltage, respectively. The rationale behind this strategy is detailed in Section 195

3.3.1. The overall hydraulic retention time (HRT) was kept at 72 hr, meaning that the 196

HRT for each module was 72 hr during in-parallel operation and 24 hr during in-series 197

operation. Schematics drawing of the operational modes can be found in Section 3.3. 198

3. Results and discussion 251

3.1. Long-term operation of a single pilot MEC 252

3.1.1. Fixed-potential inoculation allows fast start-up 253

Previous studies have suggested that anode potential directly affects biofilm 254

development. While a low anode potential thermodynamically hinders the electron 255

transfer process, a high anode potential may promote the growth of non-electroactive 256

competitors to EABs (Torres et al., 2009). In the start-up of R-single, we chose an anode 257

potential of -0.35 V vs. Ag/AgCl, as it has shown to stimulate a biofilm primarily 258

composed of electroactive Geobacter spp. However, such setting at the pilot scale 259

overloads the potentiostat, which has a current limit of 800 mA. The overload was due 260

to the charging of the electric double layer, which occurs when the electrode potential 261

changes. Therefore, we deployed a stepwise method to gradually decrease the anode 262

potential to the desired value (Fig. 2). With such a strategy, we observed a swift startup 263

with current density quickly went up to a maximum over 3 A m-2 within a week. 264

Following that, the current gradually decreased despite us regularly monitoring COD 265

concentration and replenishing substrate when COD went low. It was discovered that 266

such current decrease was due to the pH change during operation. In 22 days, the 267

cathodic pH rose to above 12, while the anodic pH dropped to 5. To address this, we 268


<!-- Page 15 -->


added the pH dosing to the recirculation loop and immediately observed an increase in 269

current, which exceeded 800 mA within 2 days. Consequently, we then switched to 270

power supply for fixed-voltage operation (Fig. 2) . 271

3.1.2. Long term performance of the R-single 281

The R-single showed good performance overall under different operational conditions. 282

The highest current density achieved was 16.6 A m-2 and 9.3 A m-2, respectively, when 283

the reactor was fed with synthetic wastewater and actual PHW-GFW, respectively (Fig. 284

3A). This current density is only slightly lower than the maximum achieved in the 285

previous lab-scale study fed with PHW (~ 20 A m-2) and exceeded that of most lab- 286

scale MECs – which typically have a current density < 10 A m-2 (Jiang et al., 2023b; 287

Tang et al., 2022). When comparing with previous pilot MECs, the current density 288

stands out as one of the highest. This is especially promising considering that low-cost 289

SS cathode was used but still warrants comparable or better current density than 290

expensive catalysts (Guerrero-Sodric et al., 2024, 2023). The high current density most 291

likely benefited from the high conductivity of the anolyte, which has been shown to 292

positively correlates with current density (Jiang et al., 2023a). Higher results have been 293

achieved, but generally on a much smaller scale and with highly saline anolyte. For 294

example, Rousseau et al., 2020b achieved a maximum of 90 A m-2 in a 6 L MEC using 295

halotolerant bioanode with highly saline anolyte (Starkey medium supplemented with 296

45 g L-1 NaCl). The reactor in this study also exhibited a high 𝑟𝑟𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐 (> 80%) and high 297

purity (> 95% in all but one measurements) of the cathodic gas (Fig. 3B) after 298

successful inhibition of methanogens and acetogens in the cathode, which will be 299

discussed in Section 3.1.3. The decrease in current density when using PHW-GFW is 300

due to the complexity of the substrate. PHW-GFW was derived from a grocery store 301

food waste mixture, which contains a variety of organic compounds such as saccharides, 302

protein, and fatty acids. The resulting PHW therefore contained organics that may not 303

be readily available to EABs, such as glycerol which is present in high concentration in 304

PHW-GFW (Table 1). Rather, they were first undergoing fermentation, with the 305

resulting fermentation products subsequently utilized by EABs. Our previous study 306

revealed the exact microbial PHW degradation process (Jiang et al., 2023b). 307

Additionally, the presence of sugars and proteins in the food waste mixture leads to the 308

formation nitrogen-containing heterocyclic compounds through Maillard reaction, 309


<!-- Page 17 -->


which is potentially toxic to EABs. The R-single reactor reliably achieved COD 310

removal above 60% within a week under synthetic wastewater (Fig. 3C). The fastest 311

kinetics was observed from day 50 to 53 where an 85% COD removal was achieved 312

within 3 days. After switching to PHW-GFW, the COD removal kinetics slowed down, 313

indicated by the gentler slope of anode COD profile (Fig. 3C). However, with an ample 314

HRT, R-single was still able to achieve > 70% COD removal under an applied voltage 315

of 0.55 V, and > 85% COD removal under 0.73 and 0.99 V. We recorded the actual 316

applied voltage on the reactor instead of directly reading the set voltage of the power 317

supply as the ohmic loss could be significant in larger scale systems due to large current. 318

319

One key advantage of MEC compared to abiotic electrolysis for H2 production is the 320

much lower energy consumption by leveraging the chemical energy embedded in 321

wastewater. This advantage holds true in pilot operation as well. The highest energy 322

consumption observed by R-single was 26 kWh kg-H2-1 under an actual applied voltage 323

of 0.99 V (Fig. 3D), which is only about half of the energy needed by a state-of- 324

technology water electrolyzer (50 kWh kg-H2-1) (Technical Targets for Proton 325

Exchange Membrane Electrolysis, n.d.). As the energy consumption is determined by 326

the input voltage and 𝑟𝑟𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐 (see Section 2.4 for derivation) and 𝑟𝑟𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐 has been relatively 327

stable, the energy consumption scales directly with the input voltage, reducing to 16 328

kWh kg-H2-1 at 0.55 V (Fig. 3D). Such low energy consumption is significant, as the 329

cost of water electrolysis is primarily driven by electricity cost. 330

331

In the HTL process, a considerable amount of nitrogen in the feedstock ends up in the 332

PHW, resulting in high nitrogen concentrations, typically in the thousands of ppm. 333

Moreover, most of the nitrogen in PHW-GFW is organic nitrogen (ORG-N), which 334

adding additional difficulty in treatment and making most existing treatment processes 335

ineffective (Table 1). We measured the nitrogen removal profile under different 336

voltages and found that the removal efficiency is positively correlated with the applied 337

voltage (Fig. 3E-F). This is mainly due to the improved removal of NH3-N at higher 338

voltages. As NH3-N can be utilized as electron donors for certain electroactive bacteria, 339

higher anode potential induced by high applied voltage would allow a swifter removal 340

H2 was converted into CH4 at latter stage (Cusick et al., 2011; He et al., 2022). Even 367

still occur due to the diffused H2 into the cathode chamber (Guerrero-Sodric et al., 369

2023). In our system, however, no methanogenesis was observed throughout the 370

operation, evidenced by zero CH4 peak identified in GC analysis and almost 100% 371

purity H2 (Fig. 3B). We believe the strong inhibition of methanogens without adding 372

inhibitors was achieved by the low pH in the cathode chamber. The optimal pH for 373

methanogens is near neutral (6.8-7.5), whereas slightly acidic pH has been shown to 374

inhibit methanogens. In our experiments, cathodic pH was gradually adjusted to 5 after 375

starting pH control (Fig. S2), which would be sufficiently acidic to inhibit growth of 376

methanogens. In addition, the lower pH of the catholyte also facilitates H2 production 377

with the abundance of protons availability. Interestingly, 𝑟𝑟𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐 still exhibits a decrease 378

down to 53% during Day 30 to Day 50, accompanied by a gradual COD increase in 379

catholyte up to 2,090 mg L-1 (Fig. 3C). Theoretically, catholyte COD should be close 380

to 0 as neither buffer (PBS) nor the dosing solution (sulfuric acid solution) would 381

contribute to COD. The CEM should also be able to block most, if not all, COD- 382

contributing ions. Therefore, two possible reasons exist for COD increase in this period: 383

1. Compromised CEM allowed crossover of co-ions (anions); 2. Acetogens growth in 384

the cathode chamber. Upon further investigation, we believe the growth of the 385

acetogens was the major factor that contributed to cathodic COD increase. This is 386


<!-- Page 21 -->


supported by several evidence. Firstly, the HPLC analysis of the catholyte revealed a 387

major peak of acetate, but no significant peak of other organics was observed. Should 388

the CEM be compromised, the catholyte COD compositions should be much more 389

complex. Secondly, the decreased 𝑟𝑟𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐 flagged that H2 was being utilized. Since 390

methanogenic behavior was not observed, the acetogens were the most likely 391

candidates for H2 utilization. Lastly, the cathode recirculation bottle also became turbid 392

during the same period (Fig. S3A-B), suggesting microbial growth. Upon examination 393

under optical microscope, we did observe short rod-shaped cells, of which many occurs 394

in pairs (Fig. S3C) – a morphology known to be possessed by Acetobacterium spp. The 395

16S rRNA gene sequencing further proved growth of acetogens in the cathodic chamber, 396

which will be discussed in Section 3.2. 397

398

Unlike methanogens, which have been a thorny issue in MEC operation, the occurrence 399

of acetogens was reported much less frequently in MEC literature (Parameswaran et al., 400

2012, 2011; Ruiz et al., 2013). Our experimental condition might have set up a niche 401

that suits acetogens but prevents methanogenic growth due to its acidic catholyte. 402

Though consuming H2 by acetogens converted CO2 to acetate make the reactor 403

practically performs microbial electrosynthesis (MES) (Bian et al., 2024), it is not the 404

goal of this study on maximizing H2 production. Accordingly, starting Day 45, we 405

further dosed down the cathodic pH to 4 in an attempt to inhibit acetogens while 406

boosting H2 production. The pH control was successful as cathodic COD started to 407

continuously decrease owing to consumption by acetate-oxidizing bacteria, and 408

consequentially the improvement of 𝑟𝑟𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐, which went back to > 80% after dosing down 409

the cathodic pH. The development of acetogens did not recur during the remaining 410

experimental period. 411

Our approach here showcased a successful inhibition of methanogens and acetogens in 413

long-term operation without dosing specific inhibitor, such as the commonly used 414

methanogen inhibitor 2-bromoethanesulfonate (BES). Besides pH effect, we also 415

believe that the high salinity partially contributed to the inhibition of these H2- 416

consuming microbes in the cathode. Because of the continuous pH dosing and 417

recirculation, the salinity of the catholyte gradually increased in the initial period, 418

mS cm-1), the microbes might not be well suited for saline environment. Most, if not 421

all, MECs fed with saline electrolyte were inoculated from saline environments, such 422

as salt marsh. 423

3.2. Spatial heterogeneity of biofilm ecology in the pilot reactor 424

We collected biofilm samples from different sections of the anodes, as well as 425

suspended samples from cathode chamber during the cathode COD anomaly period. 426

The exact location of sampling is shown in Figure 4A. All anodic samples yielded 427

sufficient reads except for sample A32. In a pilot module, the spatial heterogeneity can 428

be observed both horizontally and vertically. In the anode chamber, the upper sections 429

of each anode are exposed to higher dissolved O2 and are closer to the power source. 430

Consequently, the anode potential exhibits a slight decrease along the depth (Fig. S5), 431

Horizontally, the anodes closer to the inlet are exposed to higher COD availability than 432

those further down the length. Such spatial variability in operation acts as selection 433

pressure toward the microbiome composition. Accordingly, the sequencing results 434

showed a much higher vertical heterogeneity compared to horizontally (Fig. 4B). Most 435

notably, from depth 2 (the middle point along the depth) further down, biofilm primarily 436

composed of Geobacter spp. was formed and in some sampling points, such genus 437

could account for almost 100% abundance (samples A22-A24, A33, A34 and B12). 438

Even in the least abundant sample B34, Geobacter spp. still accounted for 45% of the 439

reads. In contrast, samples taken from the top generally showed much higher microbial 440

diversity. Aerobes and facultative anaerobes such as Rhodococcus spp. (74% 441

abundance in A12), Azospirillum spp. (48% abundance in A13) and Dysgonomonas spp. 442

(42% abundance in A11) were found in significant abundance. When aggregated to the 443

depth, we could see a clear pattern of vertical heterogeneity, where the top samples 444

showed a distinct profile from samples taken from the middle and the bottom (Fig. 4C). 445

The dominance of Geobacter spp. from the middle down to the bottom was a result 446

of two selection pressures (Fig. 4D). The decreased DO along the depth would select 447

for anaerobes and prohibit the growth of aerobes. Moreover, as the anode potential went 448

more negative along the depth, it posed a strong selection pressure for Geobacter spp. 449

and discourage the growth of non-electroactive microbes and electroactive microbes 450

that can’t survive on low electron acceptor (anode) potentials. It should also be noted 451

that the sole methanogens identified - Methanobrevibacter spp. – were only found in 452

where no methanogenic activity was found throughout the operation (Section 3.1.3). 454

The two cathode suspended samples showed the same profile – 100% 457

3.3.1. Onsite reactor performance 495

The pilot modules were directly inoculated using constant-potential control, 496

with anode potential set at -0.35 V vs Ag/AgCl reference electrode. All three reactors 497

showed rapid start-up with current density reached >1 A m-2 within three days of 498

inoculation (Fig. 6A). We believe the fast start-up was owing to the beneficial 499

temperature (30 ℃), the right inoculum from preacclimated reactors, and the proper 500

applied anode potential. The pilot modules were operated with synthetic wastewater 501

using sodium acetate until day 12, to allow for ample acclimation of the microbial 502

community. From then on, PHW-SDW diluted to a COD of 5,000 mg L-1 was used as 503

anolyte. During in-parallel operation, all three modules were exposed to the same COD 504

concentration at the inlet. As expected, R2 and R3 exhibited similar current density 505

profiles with a maximum current density of 8.7 A m-2 (Fig. 6B). R1, however, started 506

with similar current density then went through a drastic increase followed by a drop, 507

which was due to the failure of the resistor connected in the electrical circuit. As the 508

current density was derived from recording the potential drop across the resistor, the 509

change in resistance directly affected the calculated current density. Upon replacing a 510

functioning resistor on Day 16, the current density profile went back to normal. During 511

in-series operation, a tiered voltage strategy was applied, with 0.9 V for R1, 0.7 V for 512

R2 and 0.5 V for R3, respectively. The rationale was that since R1 received the highest 513


<!-- Page 29 -->


COD concentration, applying a higher voltage would ensure the optimal H2 production 514

rate. Whereas R2 and R3 were mainly used as a polishing step for the remainder COD 515

that R1 could not degrade. The tiered voltage strategy indeed resulted in a tiered current 516

density profile (Fig. 6B), where R1 reached a maximum current density of 12.5 A m-2, 517

whereas R2 and R3 current density dropped. 518

The COD concentration was measured at the outlet of each module, and COD 519

removal for each module is calculated based on the inlet and outlet COD concentrations. 520

When using synthetic wastewater, the maximum COD removal was 78.4% (Fig. 6C). 521

After switching to PHW-SDW as substrate, the COD removal decreased with the 522

maximum removal being 66.3 ± 10.6% (Fig. 6D). The in-series operation, however, 523

did show higher COD removal under the same HRT. The final effluent (outlet of R3) 524

showed a maximum COD removal of 86.4%. The improvement in COD removal is 525

likely due to better mass transfer and longer retention time, as the flow rate in in-series 526

operation is three times as fast as in-parallel operation to keep the overall HRT the same. 527

The H2 production rate follows the same pattern as current density, as the 𝑟𝑟𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐 528

was almost always > 90% throughout the onsite integration. The maximum H2 529

production rate when using synthetic wastewater was 1.1 L Lcat day-1 and increased 530

when substrate was switched to PHW-SDW (Fig. 6E-F). The increased H2 production 531

rate reflected the increased combined current of all three modules, which is likely a 532

result of the higher conductivity of the PHW-SDW compared to synthetic wastewater. 533

During in-parallel operation, the maximum H2 production rate was 1.2 L Lcat day-1. The 534


<!-- Page 30 -->


in-series operation led to tiered H2 production rate, with the highest production rate of 535

the three modules being 1.8, 0.7 and 0.7 L Lcat day-1, respectively. When normalized to 536

the reactor volume, the highest H2 production rate was 0.5 L LR day-1. To the best of 537

our knowledge, this is the highest H2 production rate achieved in pilot MECs with a 538

module volume > 10 L (Fig. S6) (Jiang et al., 2023a). In contrary to COD removal rate, 539

which does not show a clear trend with respect to reactor volume, H2 production rate 540

often drastically scale down as the reactor module increases (Jiang et al., 2023a). 541

However, it should be noted that these results were achieved with a cathodic pH set at 542

4. Theoretically, each unit decrease in cathodic pH reduces the energy requirement of 543

the MEC by 59 mV (Rousseau et al., 2020a; Ruiz et al., 2015). Therefore, a pH of 4 544

would lower the energy requirement by 0.18 V compared to neutral cathodic pH. Some 545

previous works that did not employ pH control could have cathodic pH that rose to> 546

12, leading to significant energy loss. Although pH control would inevitably add to the 547

operational cost, we believe this should be feasible as pH control in electrochemical 548

settings is well-established at industrial scale such as alkaline water electrolysis (Brauns 549

and Turek, 2020). The elevated temperature being used also partly contributed to the 550

good performance. Therefore, it is important to factor in these differences in comparing 551

performance at similar applied voltage. The use of PBS warrants further investigation 552

on the lifecycle environmental benefits, but could be minimized through selection of 553

PHW with suitable strength, and through configuration optimization. 554
